title: Screwdriver
prompt: A labelled bench teaching model of the page 32 screwdriver seats its tip in a screw in a wood block. Turn drives the screw. Reverse backs it out. Compare handles exchanges two fixed handle diameters on the same shaft while applying the same tangential hand force. The larger handle gives greater torque and requires more rim travel per turn. See-through shows the handle fixed to the shaft, tip engagement, screw head and thread in the block. Force and torque are overlays, not extra parts.
chapter: Part 1: The Mechanics of Movement / The Wheel and Axle
blurb: A bench teaching adaptation compares two fixed handle sizes to show how the same hand force gives different torque and rim travel.

identity.note: The Wheel and Axle / The Wheel and Axle at Work / Screwdriver, page 32. The 2016 image confirms the name missing from its OCR heading.
identity.mechanism: Hand effort at the broad handle produces torque on the narrow shaft and tip to turn a screw.
identity.classificationNote: Only The Wheel and Axle and Gears and Belts are main principle chapters in this unit. Other entries are named examples, diagrams or subsection headings. Greek Mill has both historical context and a named mechanism diagram.

adaptationDecision.reason: Retain as a torque-tool application. The later wood-screw row teaches thread conversion. Prior hammer and nail extractor strike or pull a nail rather than rotate a screw.

prompt.note: The screw-driving actions are faithful. Widen handle is a comparison adaptation rather than anatomy of the pictured fixed screwdriver. Make the interchangeable handle explicit and keep this lesson about torque rather than treating the screw thread as an internal screwdriver mechanism.
prompt.apparatusRelation: Named tool with an explicit interchangeable-handle teaching fixture. It does not claim the book screwdriver changes shape.

builderTruthNotes: Simple tool. Real handle, shaft, tip, screw head, screw thread and wood specimen suffice. No invented gearbox or motor.

Label all meaningful drawn real components and physical features. Distinguish force and travel overlays from anatomy. The individual builder brief must declare its expected minimum before building. No invented parts to meet a quota.
Identify the teaching adaptation in metadata, blurb and truth notes. Reset, specimen exchange, slow view and hand positioning are teaching controls rather than hidden machine hardware.

constructionResearch.claim: Internal handle flanges give a fixed twist-resistant blade anchor.
constructionResearch.scope: Representative construction, not identification of the book drawing.

truthNotes: The two fixed teaching handles exchange while stopped on the same flanged shaft; neither handle expands.
The wood specimen and board are teaching fixtures, excluded from the anatomy count.
The red hand-force arrow and dashed moment arm are overlays, excluded from anatomy.
A hand is implied to hold and follow the screwdriver; no motor or hidden support is modelled.
The screw is already started. Turn advances one turn at 1.5 mm pitch; Reverse returns toward the initial started position. Eight turns stop before seating.

At constant 20 N tangential effort, 12 and 24 mm handle radii produce 0.24 and 0.48 Nm. Rim travel is 75 and 151 mm per turn. Motion is prescribed for teaching, not a friction or cutting-force simulation.
1988 remains inaccessible and unverified. No edition-union claim.
Nine labels name tool and screw anatomy. WOOD SPECIMEN and BENCH BOARD label teaching fixtures and do not count toward anatomy.
